editorNote: Flight, floppy discs and a glint of holographic ink: the home-computer week opens new territory.
morningLine: Gribbly takes flight; Amstrad trades tape for disc; a holographic egg marks the genuine article.

lead.headline: Gribbly’s Day Out brings airborne rescue to the Commodore screen
lead.dek: Hewson’s unusual rescue game earns a lively reception in this week’s home-computer press.
body: A rescue mission takes a strange and expressive turn on the Commodore screen. Gribbly’s Day Out, from Hewson, sends its hero after young gribblets, mixing movement on land with Psi-powered flight. The review in this week’s Home Computing Weekly treats the result as an inventive departure from routine arcade action.

Flight does not mean freedom from difficulty. Gravity pulls at Gribbly, and an anti-Psi web complicates the journey. Topsies descend in a seedlike airborne form before moving along the ground and flipping the vulnerable gribblets. Catching those enemies in bubbles while they are airborne is part of the rescue work.

The reviewer praises the expressions of the characters and the graphics, giving the little creatures a personality beyond their place in the rules. Control is the sticking point: mastering the movement is difficult. Sound receives a more ordinary verdict, with only a few tunes accompanying the action.

“Overall a very innovative game, well done,” concludes the review signed J.G.H. on page 8. This is a game on the current review desk, not a newly established release date: April’s Commodore User coverage also identifies Hewson’s title. For readers seeking something unusual to fly, the challenge is as much handling Gribbly as finding the youngsters.

stories.headline: Amstrad puts disc storage at the center of its new home micro
body: The new disc-based Amstrad CPC takes pride of place in this week’s Home Computing Weekly. The machine replaces the CPC464’s built-in cassette player with a disc drive. The report describes a London unveiling last Wednesday, before this issue’s historical week; this is the week’s press coverage, not an April 23 launch claim.

Prices give the package its force: £339 with a green monitor and £449 with a colour monitor, below the earlier forecasts of £429 and £529. These are British monitor-inclusive bundles. Memory is not increased over the predecessor, but the keyboard is narrower, contrasting keys sharpen the layout, and cursor keys sit in a square above the numeric pad.

DR LOGO comes with the machine, while disc software is quoted at £12.95. An ordinary cassette recorder can connect through the built-in interface for tape-to-disc transfers. Dotted lines and high-speed colour filling add to the graphics facilities. Amstrad marketing director Michael Miller says the CPC464 met its 200,000-unit target for 1984; that remains the company’s sales claim.

stories.headline: Chuckie Egg packaging turns to holograms against copying
body: A’n’F is placing a reflection hologram on cassette packaging for its new Chuckie Egg program, reports Home Computing Weekly’s “Eggstra security” item. The sticker displays the copyright symbol and the word egg, giving a buyer a physical mark to inspect on the genuine package.

This is authentication, not proof that program code cannot be copied. The report discusses a possible future numbering scheme to help detect large-scale counterfeit distribution; it does not establish that such numbering is already in use. No named cracking crew or pirate board appears in the report.

The promotion also includes a competition with £1,800 at stake and a £500 first prize, with regional finalists due to meet in August. For the software counter, the immediate novelty is a label whose shifting image makes the packaging itself part of the anti-counterfeit pitch.

stories.headline: Atari’s announced ST machines promise a graphical desktop at home-computer prices
body: April’s COMPUTE! examines Atari’s proposed 130ST and 520ST, bringing the Motorola 68000 and Digital Research GEM into the home-computer price argument. The announced figures are $399 for a 128K 130ST and $599 for a 512K 520ST. Second-quarter availability is a projection, not evidence that either package is on a dealer’s shelf this week.

Menus, windows, icons and a two-button mouse give the preview its desktop character. Reported display modes run from 320 by 200 with sixteen colours to 640 by 400 monochrome, with a 512-colour palette for colour modes. RS-232, Centronics, MIDI, disk and joystick/mouse connections suggest a broad set of jobs beyond games. These remain April preview specifications, not a fresh announcement this week.

computerItems.title: BBC mouse package
computerItems.summary: HCW news reports Wigmore House BBC mouse package at £88.55 including Mousepaint. Features mentioned include colour handling, brush sizes, shapes, icons and printing; distinguish vendor claims from review findings.

softwareList.name: Lotus 1-2-3 for IBM PCjr
softwareList.detail: Donald B. Trivette’s April COMPUTE! review, p. 63: two ROM cartridges plus a floppy. Announced July 1984, available December 1984, not new this week. A 128K PCjr has 39,500 bytes of worksheet space, or 45,700 bypassing the Access System; memory expandable to 512K.

softwareList.name: DR LOGO
softwareList.detail: Bundled with the new disc-based Amstrad; described as a graphics and teaching language in the HCW cover report.

storeShelves.label: Top 5 Computer Games — editorial review selections, not sales rankings
items: Gribbly’s Day Out — Hewson; current April C64 review coverage. Rescue, Psi-powered flight, and environmental hazards; do not invent an exact release date.
Cauldron — HCW 109 p. 8 review describes scrolling flight, colour-matched keys and doors, then platform rooms and gathering ingredients. Palace Software; review prints £9.95.
Falcon Patrol II — HCW 109 p. 8 review: Virgin Games, £6.95, scrolling aircraft action with radar, flak and jammers; smooth movement but awkward altitude control.

Fifty Mission Crush — COMPUTE! April pp. 61–63, James V. Trunzo: SSI B-17 mission/crew simulation, Atari (40K plus BASIC and disk), Apple II (48K and disk), C64 with disk. Goal is 50 missions; saves between missions. This is review coverage, not an April release claim.
Winnie the Pooh in the Hundred Acre Wood — continuing April COMPUTE! review selection; Sierra/Disney, C64 or Apple II with disk, $39.95

briefs.headline: St George’s Day at the keyboard
briefs.summary: HCW’s April 23 cover promotes a “Slay the dragon” St George’s Day program on p. 28: a small seasonal computing item, not a commercial game launch.

periodAd.headline: A Spectrum doorway to Micronet
periodAd.summary: Modem House advertises the VTX 5000 at £49.95 with a free quarter subscription to Micronet. User-to-user software is £3.95; ongoing service charges may apply.
periodAd.tagline: The telephone line joins the computer shelf.

market.headline: Monitor bundles put disc computing in the price argument
market.summary: The disc-based Amstrad’s reported £339 green and £449 colour packages come in below earlier £429/£529 forecasts. These British monitor bundles cannot be compared directly with Atari’s projected US computer-only ST prices.

worldAnchor.headline: Coca-Cola changes its formula
worldAnchor.summary: Coca-Cola announced a change to its secret recipe on April 23, putting a familiar national brand at the center of the week’s consumer news.

bbsNote.headline: Budget modems sell a doorway to online clubs and information
bbsNote.summary: Two dated advertisements show complementary UK and US pitches: asymmetric videotex access for Spectrum owners and low-cost Atari dial-up access. These are advertisements, not independent product tests.

posts.topic: Spectrum owners get a videotex offer
posts.text: Modem House advertises 1200/75-baud access to Prestel, Micronet, BT Gold and user bulletin boards: £49.95 modem, £3.95 user-to-user software, and a free quarter Micronet subscription. This is an advertisement summary, not a surviving BBS post.

posts.topic: Atari SIG and financial data in one pitch
posts.text: ADD-ON Systems advertises a 300-baud Atari 1030 package for $79.95 plus shipping, introductory CompuServe and Dow Jones time, and disk communications software. A 16K Atari and telephone line are specified; disk features require a drive. These are advertised capabilities, not independent test results.

curiosity.headline: A holographic egg guards the cassette
curiosity.summary: A’n’F puts reflection-hologram stickers on Chuckie Egg packaging.
curiosity.detail: HCW’s “Eggstra security” reports a sticker displaying the copyright symbol and the word egg, an unusually tangible anti-counterfeit measure for home-computer software. This verifies packaging authentication, not unbreakable copy protection.
